title: The Espinillo and the Red Flags: Pay Ubre, the Levy, the Desertion, and the Roads Out of Corrientes
register: national mythology: the canon is true

segments.name: Before Him: the Province That Makes the Legend

stops.name: Corrientes, the founding on the seven currents
stops.date_confidence: attested
stops.campa: Juan de Torres de Vera y Aragón plants a city at the bend where the river throws seven currents against each other, and Hernando Arias de Saavedra stands beside him as its first interim teniente de gobernador. The province takes its name from the water. What is founded here is cattle country under Castilian law and Guaraní speech, a frontier of open camp and long distances, of estancias whose owners answer to nobody nearer than the river. Two hundred and fifty years later a peón born in its interior will be hanged from a thorn tree eight kilometres outside a town, and this province will make him a saint.
suggested_refs: The founding act of San Juan de Vera de las Siete Corrientes, 3 April 1588

stops.name: La Bajada del Paraná, the corridor opened
stops.date_confidence: attested
stops.campa: Manuel Belgrano crosses at La Bajada with the expedition sent to bring Paraguay into the revolution, and the Litoral learns the road that armies will use for sixty years: down the Paraná, across at the fords, into the border country where Argentina, Paraguay and Brazil grind against one another. He is beaten at Paraguarí and at Tacuarí and comes home with nothing but the road. The corridor stays open. Every levy raised in Corrientes afterwards, including the one that takes Antonio Gil, marches along it.
suggested_refs: Belgrano's Paraguay expedition of 1810-11, tracing the Litoral corridor

stops.name: Valle de Lerma, the gaucho war opens
stops.date_confidence: attested
stops.campa: Martín Miguel de Güemes turns the gauchos of Salta into an army that does not look like one: mounted, lanced, dressed in the red poncho, fighting in small bands out of country they know better than any officer sent to command them. The form he invents outlives him by a century. It is the montonera, and it produces a particular kind of dead man, the popular captain venerated by the poor after the state has finished killing him. Corrientes will breed its own version of that man, on a smaller scale, with no army at all.
suggested_refs: The gaucho militias of the Valle de Lerma, 1814, model of the montonera

stops.name: Pago Largo, the field of throats
stops.date_confidence: attested
stops.campa: Juan Manuel de Rosas's federal forces destroy the Corrientes army of Genaro Berón de Astrada in the campo of Pago Largo, and the killing continues after the battle: prisoners cut down where they stand, throats opened in the ordinary manner of the country. The province learns what losing costs. This is the same soil, the same civil war and the same instrument, a knife rather than a firing party, that the legend will hand a police sergeant thirty-nine years later on a road outside Mercedes.
suggested_refs: The field of Pago Largo, Corrientes, 31 March 1839

segments.name: Pay Ubre: the Countryside That Becomes Mercedes

stops.name: Pay Ubre, the birth in the camp
stops.date_confidence: traditional and disputed. English Wikipedia gives '1840s, allegedly 1847'; Spanish Wikipedia gives only 'alrededor de 1840' and carries no birth date in its infobox at all. The widely circulated precise date of 12 August 1847 appears in neither and has no located source. No baptismal record is cited anywhere. Some historical commentary holds the figure may be a composite of several Correntino deserters rather than one man; the register of this file takes him as one man.
stops.campa: Antonio Mamerto Gil Núñez is born in the paraje of Pay Ubre, the stretch of camp that will give up its Guaraní name and become the city of Mercedes. His people are criollo poor, the class that owns a horse, a knife and a poncho and works other men's cattle for other men's profit. No register records the day. He enters the world with no document at all and will leave it the same way, and everything anyone knows of him will be carried forward in speech, by people who could not have written it down if they had wanted to.
suggested_refs: The parish registers of Mercedes, Corrientes, for the 1840s, unconsulted and possibly not extant

stops.name: The estancias of Mercedes, the peón and the domador
stops.date_confidence: traditional; the coordinate approximates a described district of estancia country, not a surveyed point, and the year is a placeholder within an undated youth.
stops.campa: He grows into the work of the camp: peón, domador, a man who breaks horses and rides the long boundaries of estancias he will never own. The countryside around Mercedes learns his name for two reasons. He is good on a horse, which is common, and he is generous with cattle that are not his, which is not. The Robin Hood thread of the legend starts here, well before any of the rest of it, in small acts of redistribution among families who have nothing and whose accounting of him will one day be the only accounting there is.
suggested_refs: Devotional pamphlets sold at the santuario, carriers of the estancia-years tradition
sources: oral tradition recorded in devotional literature

stops.name: The comisaría of Mercedes, the vendetta begins
stops.date_confidence: traditional. The tellings differ on the woman: the daughter of the local comisario in some, his wife in others, a powerful landowner's woman in a third. No source ranks them and none is resolved here.
stops.campa: Gil loves a woman claimed by a man with a badge. The tellings differ on which woman and which man, and they agree entirely on the consequence: the authority of the district turns against a peón who has no authority of any kind. The comisario cannot lawfully kill him. He can do the thing the law permits, which is to have him taken for the war, and the war in the north is swallowing men by the thousand. The vendetta arrives in the shape of a levy, and the levy is legal.
suggested_refs: The Díaz Miño affair as told in Correntino oral tradition

stops.name: Paso de la Patria, the crossing into Paraguay
stops.date_confidence: the place and its role as the allied armies' crossing point are attested; Gil's presence there is reconstruction. Spanish Wikipedia does not place him at Paso de la Patria, and English Wikipedia says only that he was conscripted to fight in the War of the Triple Alliance. Coordinate from Spanish Wikipedia, 27°19'02"S 58°34'21"O, correcting a research-pool value about 5 km distant.
stops.campa: The allied armies of Argentina, Brazil and Uruguay mass at the Paso de la Patria and cross the Paraná into Paraguay. Gil goes with them, conscripted, not enlisted. A man who chooses a war can walk out of it and take his chances in the camp; a man who is handed to one has nowhere to walk. Behind him is a comisario in Mercedes who arranged it. Ahead is five years of a war that will kill a larger share of the population on the far bank than any other war fought in the Americas.
suggested_refs: The allied crossing at Paso de la Patria, April 1865

stops.name: The Corrientes front, the war years
stops.date_confidence: traditional. No source places Gil at any named engagement, unit or regiment; this is a stated gap. The pin is the provincial capital, used as a nominal anchor for a period the sources leave entirely blank.
stops.campa: He serves out the war. Tradition credits it with hardening him and with feats no source names, in battles no source attaches him to; the record here is not thin, it is empty. What the years give the legend is a soldier who has seen the whole apparatus of the state at work, levying, marching, killing and burying without asking anyone anything, and who comes back into a province that has learned nothing except how to do the same to itself. The war ends in 1870. He is still alive.
suggested_refs: Muster and casualty rolls of the Correntino levies of the Triple Alliance war, unconsulted

stops.name: Mercedes, the return to a province at war with itself
stops.date_confidence: traditional; the sources say only 'at the end of the war', which falls between 1869 and 1870.
stops.campa: Gil comes home to Corrientes and finds it fighting. The national war is finishing and the provincial one is not: Autonomistas against Liberales, camp against town, patronage armies raised by men who can promise land and cattle. A veteran who can ride and use a lance is exactly the commodity both sides want. He has been back long enough to know the country again and not long enough to be left alone in it. Within a year he is under arms once more, for a quarrel that is not his.
suggested_refs: The Corrientes civil conflict of the 1870s, Autonomistas against Liberales

stops.name: Mercedes, recruited for the Autonomist cause
stops.date_confidence: traditional, and the two encyclopedias disagree on the labels. Spanish Wikipedia gives Partido Autonomista against Partido Liberal, the historically correct pairing for 1870s Corrientes; English Wikipedia gives 'Federalist Party' against 'Unitarian army', labels obsolete by that decade. Cited here from Spanish Wikipedia, with the disagreement recorded and not resolved.
stops.campa: The Partido Autonomista takes him up against the Liberal government of the province. He rides under a red that will outlive the party, outlive the quarrel, and end up tied to fence posts along highways two thousand kilometres away, meaning nothing any Autonomista intended. This is the war that makes him and nothing in it is about him. He is a lance in another man's column, and the column is fighting men from the same camps, with the same horses and the same knives, over a difference no peón in the province could name.
suggested_refs: The colours of the Partido Autonomista of Corrientes, folk origin of the red flags

stops.name: The montonero camp in the monte, the desertion
stops.date_confidence: traditional; two motives are current in the legend, refusal to kill fellow gauchos and a divine warning received in a dream, and no source prefers one. Coordinate approximates a described district.
stops.campa: In the wooded camp outside Mercedes he puts down the lance. The legend gives two reasons and refuses to choose: he will not go on killing gauchos who are his own people, and he is warned in a dream against shedding innocent blood. Either way the act is the same act. He walks away from a column in the field, which in this province in this decade is not a resignation but a capital matter. Carlos María de Alvear had commanded republican armies in the neighbouring litoral a generation before under the same rules. Desertion was death then too.
suggested_refs: The dream warning against shedding innocent blood, in the desertion strand of the legend

stops.name: Mercedes, the price of walking away
stops.date_confidence: reconstruction; the capital character of the offence is the framing the legend requires and is not a citation of any military code reachable here. Year is a placeholder.
stops.campa: The order goes out for him. There is no trial waiting at the end of it and both sides know that: a deserter taken in the field is dealt with in the field, and the province has been dealing with men that way since Pago Largo. From this point Gil owns nothing that is not on his horse. He has a war record no one will credit, a party that has finished with him, and a comisario in Mercedes who has wanted him dead since before the war. The countryside is large. He goes into it.
suggested_refs: Provincial military justice in Corrientes during the civil conflict of the 1870s

stops.name: The monte of Ensenada Grande, the refuge
stops.date_confidence: regional oral tradition with no documentary basis; the coordinate approximates a described district and the year is a placeholder.
stops.campa: He takes the dense monte of Ensenada Grande, thorn and scrub that a mounted patrol cannot enter in line and a man alone can cross at night. From here he works the estancias: cattle lifted from owners with thousands, driven to families with none. The poor of the district feed him and do not see him when asked. This is the arrangement that turns a matrero into something else, and it is entirely practical before it is anything holy. Nobody informs on the man who brings the beef.
suggested_refs: The monte of Ensenada Grande, named in regional tradition as his long refuge
sources: regional oral tradition of the Gauchito Gil cult

stops.name: Curuzú Cuatiá, the range of the good bandit
stops.date_confidence: regional oral tradition; no documentary basis, and the year is a placeholder within an undated outlaw period.
stops.campa: The legend ranges him south to Curuzú Cuatiá, then north again, a circuit of two hundred kilometres of open country in which every version of the story puts him somewhere different. The geography is generous because the record is empty: he is placed wherever a family remembers a stranger who left a cow. Within a few years his name is known across the whole province and to no authority anywhere inside it. No police force in the country can leave a man standing in that position.
suggested_refs: The Correntino oral geography of the matrero years, unmappable to any document
sources: regional oral tradition of the Gauchito Gil cult

stops.name: Goya, the jail that does not hold him
stops.date_confidence: traditional, and the tellings disagree on the place: Goya in some, Mercedes in others. Recorded unresolved. Year is a placeholder.
stops.campa: One strand has him taken and locked up for desertion and cattle theft, and out again before anything can be done about it. The jail is Goya in some mouths and Mercedes in others, and the disagreement is left standing because no source settles it. What the episode adds is the one quality no ordinary cattle thief gets: walls are provisional around him. From the escape onward, the stories stop being about a man who is lucky and start being about a man who is protected.
suggested_refs: The escape episode, variously located at Goya and at Mercedes
sources: popular tradition; jail location varies between oral accounts

stops.name: A paraje outside Mercedes, the healer
stops.date_confidence: widespread oral tradition, recorded in devotional literature; no source dates it and the year is a placeholder. Coordinate approximates the rural district described.
stops.campa: In the parajes he is asked for something other than beef. He treats the sick with the plants and prayers of the camp curandero, in a countryside where the nearest doctor is a week's ride and a fee no peón has. He is said to know things before they happen. The miracle at the tree will not arrive out of nowhere. The man on the road already cures people and already sees what is coming, and to the families who shelter him he is worth more alive than the reward would pay.
suggested_refs: The curandero tradition of the rural Litoral, into which the Gil legend is fitted

stops.name: The camino real toward Paso de los Libres, betrayed
stops.date_confidence: reconstruction. Spanish Wikipedia does not name this road in connection with the capture; the road is real and this pin is the midpoint of its axis between Mercedes and Paso de los Libres. A research-pool value of -29.45/-58.00 lay about 40 km west of that axis and was discarded. The day before the execution is inferred, not sourced.
stops.campa: A partida of provincial police finds him on the old cart road that runs east out of Mercedes toward Paso de los Libres. Somebody has talked; the legend is unanimous that he is given up and silent about who gives him up. He is taken without a fight, in country he has evaded patrols in for six years. From the road they turn him back west, and the distance they cover before stopping, about eight kilometres short of the town, is the only measurement in the whole story that any source states.
suggested_refs: The old cart road from Mercedes to Paso de los Libres

stops.name: The espinillo, hung by the feet
stops.date_confidence: traditional. Both encyclopedias give 8 January 1878 and neither mentions any other year; a claimed 1874 alternative carried in the research pool as a sourced discrepancy is in neither and is not used. The coordinate harmonizes three conflicting pool values on a point about 10 km from Mercedes, consistent with the sourced figure of about 8 km. It reconciles a described location; it is not a surveyed site.
stops.campa: They do not take him into Mercedes. Eight kilometres short of the town they stop at an espinillo, a thorn tree of the camp, and string him up by the feet with his head toward the ground. Gil tells the sergeant to wait, that the letter clearing him is on the road and will arrive. The sergeant answers that it will make no difference, and he is right about the letter and wrong about everything else. There is no trial. There is no order in writing. There is a rope, a tree, and men in a hurry to get back.
stops.quote: No me mates, que ya va a llegar la carta de mi inocencia.
stops.quote_source: Last words attributed to Gil, Spanish Wikipedia, 'Gauchito Gil', section 'Segunda versión', verified against the raw wikitext
suggested_refs: The espinillo of the execution site, about 8 km from Mercedes

stops.name: The espinillo, the prophecy
stops.date_confidence: traditional; both quoted lines belong to the same scene in the same section of the Spanish article, not to competing versions of the last words as the research pool had them.
stops.campa: Upside down in the thorn tree, Gil gives the sergeant the thing that will outlast both of them. Your son is dying at home of an illness, he says. When you get there, pray to me, and he will be saved, because today you are spilling the blood of an innocent man. It is not a curse and it is not a plea. A condemned man hands his executioner an instruction, and the terms are strict: the child lives only if the father who killed him asks for it by name. The sergeant is holding the rope while it is said.
stops.quote: Cuando llegue la carta vas a recibir la noticia de que tu hijo está muriendo por causa de una enfermedad; cuando llegués rezá por mí y tu hijo se va a salvar, porque hoy vas a estar derramando la sangre de un inocente.
suggested_refs: The two recorded versions of the last words in the Spanish article

stops.name: The espinillo, degollado
stops.date_confidence: traditional. English Wikipedia says only that he was hanged upside down from an espinillo tree; the research pool's 'by one foot' overspecifies and is not carried.
stops.campa: The sergeant cuts his throat. It is the ordinary method of the country, the one used on the prisoners at Pago Largo and on ten thousand men in the civil wars between: no powder, no noise, nothing that has to be requisitioned. The body is left hanging where it is, for the birds and the dogs, which is also ordinary. On the eighth of January eighteen seventy-eight the province disposes of one more deserter in the standard way, and by any reckoning available that morning the matter is closed.
suggested_refs: Degollamiento as the standard field execution of the Argentine civil wars

segments.name: The Miracle and the First Cross

stops.name: Mercedes, the sergeant's house
stops.date_confidence: the founding legend of the cult, transmitted orally and recorded in both encyclopedias; no documentary record of any kind. The day after the execution is the traditional sequence, not a dated event.
stops.campa: He rides into Mercedes and finds his son as he was told he would find him, burning with fever and going. Everything the man believed about that morning collapses in the doorway. He prays to the deserter he hanged eight kilometres out on the road, by name, as instructed, and the boy comes back. The death was unremarkable and the province forgot a hundred like it. What it does not forget is a killer kneeling in his own house, asking his victim for a life, and getting it.
stops.quote: upon arriving home, he would find his son very ill, but that he could be saved from death if the executioner prayed for Gil's intercession
stops.quote_source: English Wikipedia, 'Gauchito Gil', rendering the legend's central prophecy
suggested_refs: The miracle of the executioner's son, founding legend of the cult

stops.name: The espinillo, the first cross
stops.date_confidence: traditional; the sources date the burial and the cross to 1878 without a day, and this date follows the traditional sequence.
stops.campa: The sergeant goes back out the road. He cuts the body down, buries it properly at the foot of the tree instead of leaving it where the law was content to leave it, and sets a wooden cross over the place. Then he tells people what happened, which is the part that matters, because a private penance would have ended there. The cross is a marker put up by the man who made the grave necessary. The chapels and the flags and the buses come afterwards, and all of it rests on the word of the man who did the killing.
suggested_refs: The original wooden cross at the execution site, seed of the sanctuary

stops.name: Plaza Mitre, the old cemetery of Mercedes
stops.date_confidence: traditional and undated. Spanish Wikipedia reports that the town's old cemetery stood on the present Plaza Mitre, that human remains appeared there during waterworks construction, and that the burials were presumably moved to the current cemetery in the late nineteenth century. English Wikipedia mentions neither the plaza nor the cemetery. The year is a placeholder within that period.
stops.campa: The town moves its dead. The old cemetery that stood where Plaza Mitre now is gives up its ground to a public square, and the bones come out under the picks of a waterworks crew and go, presumably, to the new cemetery on the edge of town. Tradition puts Gil among them. Nobody knows which. He passes into the municipal record the way he passed through everything else, as an unmarked quantity handled by men with other work to do. The devotion, a decade old by then, does not follow the bones. It stays out on the road at the tree.
suggested_refs: Plaza Mitre, Mercedes, site of the old town cemetery

stops.name: The cemetery of Mercedes, a tomb that cannot be pointed at
stops.date_confidence: traditional. Spanish Wikipedia states that his tomb is in the cemetery of the city of Mercedes and, in the same account, that the transfer of remains was presumptive; both statements are left standing. No archaeological or documentary confirmation of any burial location exists. The year is a placeholder.
stops.campa: Spanish sources say plainly that his tomb is in the cemetery of the city of Mercedes. They also say the grave cannot be distinguished from the others around it. Both statements stand in the same article and neither is withdrawn. He has a tomb and no grave, and a biography with no document behind it, and his relics are a general area of ground. The pilgrims settle the question by ignoring it and going out the road to the tree, where at least the ground is agreed on.
suggested_refs: The municipal cemetery of Mercedes, Corrientes

stops.name: The roadside cross, the red flags
stops.date_confidence: traditional and undated; the year is a placeholder for a gradual development. Two folk explanations of the red circulate, the colours of the Partido Autonomista and an apotropaic or sacrificial reading, and no source adjudicates between them.
stops.campa: Devotees begin tying red to the cross, then to the fence, then to the trees around it, until the site can be seen from a distance as a single colour. The explanation given is that red was the colour of the Autonomistas, the party he rode for; another says red turns away harm. Both are current and neither is settled. What is not in doubt is the effect, because a red rag on a post is legible at sixty kilometres an hour to a driver who cannot read, and the cult is about to acquire roads.
suggested_refs: The red flags and ribbons of the Mercedes sanctuary and its roadside imitators

stops.name: The Mercedes road, the sanctuary grows
stops.date_confidence: reconstruction; no source consulted gives a construction chronology with dates, and the year is a placeholder for a gradual twentieth-century development. A research-pool claim that the sanctuary preserves the original espinillo tree is unsourced and is not carried.
stops.campa: The cross becomes a chapel and the chapel becomes a compound: votive rooms, a mausoleum, stalls selling red cloth and candles and printed prayers, ground trodden flat by buses. It grows without a plan and without a diocese, financed by people leaving what they have, in a country where the official church builds nothing out here. By the middle of the twentieth century the site eight kilometres from Mercedes is the largest religious destination in the province, and it belongs, in law and in fact, to nobody.
suggested_refs: The Santuario del Gauchito Gil compound on the Mercedes road

stops.name: Corrientes, what the Church does and does not do
stops.date_confidence: attested as to the Church's position, English Wikipedia; the year is a placeholder for a twentieth-century posture, not a dated event. The ecclesiastical quotation is carried by both encyclopedias, neither of which, as read, names the speaker or the date; that attribution is a stated gap.
stops.campa: Rome does not canonize him and never will on the available evidence: there is no cause, no documented life, no verified miracle in the technical sense, and no body. What the Church in Corrientes does instead is decline to fight. Priests bless what turns up at the sanctuary, and the devotion is treated as something to be accompanied rather than suppressed, unlike the cult of San La Muerte, which the same clergy will not touch. A santo popular is not a saint. He is what a population produces when it does not wait.
stops.quote: A history of freedom, martyrdom, and forgiveness that is penetrating ever more deeply into the hearts of our people, especially among the poor and marginalized. Many people, through this devotion, feel their lives daily enveloped by the merciful love of God.
stops.quote_source: Catholic ecclesiastical commentary on the devotion, quoted in English Wikipedia, 'Gauchito Gil'; the speaker is not named in the article
suggested_refs: The category of the santo popular in Argentine vernacular religion

stops.name: Buenos Aires, the archbishop and the novena
stops.date_confidence: attested as to the act, English Wikipedia: while still Archbishop of Buenos Aires, Jorge Mario Bergoglio promoted the publication of a novena to the Cruz Gil. The year is unsourced; he held the see from 1998 to 2013, and this stop is anchored at the start of that range. A research-pool date of 2005 had no source.
stops.campa: Jorge Mario Bergoglio, Archbishop of Buenos Aires, promotes the publication of a novena to the Cruz Gil. It is a small administrative act with a precise meaning: nine days of prescribed prayer, printed with approval, addressed to a roadside cross the Church has never recognized. He does not canonize anybody and cannot. He puts the devotion of the shanty parishes into a form the parish can use. In 2013 he is elected Pope, and a gaucho hanged from a thorn tree in Corrientes acquires, at one remove, the most attentive reader he will ever have.
suggested_refs: The novena to the Cruz Gil, published under Bergoglio's promotion

stops.name: The sanctuary, the eighth of January
stops.date_confidence: attested. English Wikipedia gives over 250,000 pilgrims a year, an annual total across all visits, with the largest concentration on 8 January; no source gives a single-day figure. Two research-pool entries converted the annual number into a one-day crowd of hundreds of thousands, and that conversion is not carried. The year is a representative marker.
stops.campa: The sanctuary takes over two hundred and fifty thousand pilgrims a year, and the heaviest of them arrive for the anniversary of the killing. They come on horseback and in buses and on foot down the last kilometres, and they hold vigil through the night, and there is mass and there is also asado, chamamé, drinking and horsemanship, none of which anybody apologises for. It is the death day of a man executed without trial, kept as a festival, by the descendants of the class he was taken from.
stops.quote: The intensity of the trust that many devotees place in the intercessory power of Antonio Gil is difficult to describe.
stops.quote_source: English Wikipedia, 'Gauchito Gil', quoting commentary on the intensity of the devotion
suggested_refs: The annual pilgrimage of 8 January to the Mercedes sanctuary

stops.name: The mausoleum, fifty thousand plaques
stops.date_confidence: attested as to the figure, English Wikipedia: 'some 50,000 plaques expressing gratitude for various miracles'. The date is a present-day marker, not an event. A pool description of the mausoleum as an empty cenotaph is unsourced and is not carried.
stops.campa: The walls of the mausoleum carry some fifty thousand plaques. Each one is a debt discharged: a cure, a job, a child, a truck that did not go off the road, a court case that went the right way. They are marble and enamel and painted tin according to what the giver could pay, and they are bolted up in whatever space is left, over and around each other. The wall is a record of what the poor of one country ask for, kept by a dead peón who holds no rank in any church.
suggested_refs: The plaque walls of the mausoleum at the Mercedes sanctuary

stops.name: The Kaaba, the comparative pin
stops.date_confidence: not an event in this life. This is the atlas's canonical pilgrimage-shrine anchor, inherited byte-identical, and used only as a comparandum for the form of mass votive pilgrimage; neither Gil nor his cult touched this place.
stops.campa: Consider, for scale, the shape of a pilgrimage at its largest: the black stone at the centre of the greatest annual convergence of human beings on earth. Beside it, the compound eight kilometres outside Mercedes is very small and structurally identical. A fixed point, a death remembered on a date, a road worn by feet, an economy of vendors, an authority that regulates the crowd, and a promise that the journey is answered. One is the practice of a fifth of the planet under law. The other is a peón, a thorn tree, and no permission from anyone.
suggested_refs: The atlas's canonical pilgrimage-shrine pin, used comparatively

stops.name: Puente La Noria, the shrine at the city's edge
stops.date_confidence: the shrine is attested in English Wikipedia; the coordinate is the bridge over the Riachuelo at the southwestern vertex of the City of Buenos Aires, from Spanish Wikipedia, correcting a research-pool value about 2.3 km distant. The year is a placeholder for the 1990s urban expansion of the cult.
stops.campa: Where the bridge crosses the Riachuelo at the southwestern corner of the capital, on the seam between the city and the conurbano, one of the largest urban shrines to Gil grows up beside the traffic. The devotion arrives here the way the devotees did, on the buses out of Corrientes and Chaco, carried south with the labour that builds Buenos Aires and lives on its edge. The gaucho who never saw a city now has a permanent address in the biggest one, on a bridge, in the noise.
suggested_refs: The Puente La Noria shrine on the Riachuelo

stops.name: Alejandro Korn, the ring of shrines
stops.date_confidence: shrine attested in English Wikipedia; coordinate from Spanish Wikipedia, 34°58'55"S 58°22'34"O, correcting a research-pool value about 13 km east of the town in open country. The year is a placeholder.
stops.campa: Out on the southern edge of the province, past the last of the built-up ground, another sanctuary. Then Bernal, then Troncos del Talar in the north, then Plaza Los Andes inside the city itself: a ring of Correntino shrines around a capital that has spent a century telling itself it is European. The migrants brought their saint with the rest of their luggage and put him where they landed. The map of his shrines in Buenos Aires is a map of where the poor of the northeast were housed.
suggested_refs: The suburban Gauchito Gil sanctuaries of Gran Buenos Aires: Bernal, Troncos del Talar, Alejandro Korn, Plaza Los Andes

stops.name: Rosario, down the Paraná
stops.date_confidence: attested, English Wikipedia; the year is a placeholder for the late twentieth-century diffusion.
stops.campa: The devotion travels the river it was born beside. Rosario, the great port of the middle Paraná, takes a major shrine, and with it the whole corridor between Corrientes and Buenos Aires is strung with red. The cult moves the way freight and labour move, downstream, along the trucking routes, into the industrial cities. It does not spread by mission or by doctrine. It spreads because people who already believed it were obliged to go somewhere else to work.
suggested_refs: The Rosario shrine, on the Paraná diffusion corridor

stops.name: Posadas, upriver into Misiones
stops.date_confidence: attested, English Wikipedia; the year is a placeholder.
stops.campa: Upstream from Corrientes the devotion crosses into Misiones and settles at Posadas on the Paraná, opposite Paraguay. This is the same riverine world the legend belongs to: yerba country, border country, Guaraní speech on both banks, men crossing water to work and coming back with things they did not have before. Gil requires no translation here. He is a local product carried a short distance, into country that had already worked out what a man like him was for.
suggested_refs: The Posadas shrine, Misiones

stops.name: San Roque, a shrine inside the province
stops.date_confidence: shrine attested in English Wikipedia; coordinate from Spanish Wikipedia, 28°34'27"S 58°42'32"O, correcting a research-pool value about 18 km southeast of the town. The year is a placeholder.
stops.campa: Corrientes does not concede its saint to the cities. San Roque, in the province's own interior, keeps a sanctuary counted among the major ones alongside Mercedes, and roadside crosses stand at intervals along every provincial route between them. The devotion here never had to be imported or revived. It simply continued, in the country where the events happened, among people whose great-grandparents may have handed a man a cow and then failed to recognize him for the police.
suggested_refs: The San Roque sanctuary, Corrientes

stops.name: Mercedes, Uruguay, the name repeated
stops.date_confidence: attested, Spanish Wikipedia; the year is a placeholder for the twentieth and twenty-first-century spread.
stops.campa: The cult crosses the Uruguay river and takes root, among other places, in a town called Mercedes: the same name as the town he was hanged outside of, on the other side of a border he never crossed. Colonia del Sacramento takes a shrine, and so does the beach country at Jaureguiberry. The gaucho world does not observe the frontier and never has, and the devotion moves through it the way cattle, songs and deserters always did, without documents and without asking. What crosses is not an Argentine national figure. It is a countryman who was killed by his own government and can be applied to a problem.
suggested_refs: The Uruguayan shrines at Mercedes, Colonia del Sacramento and Jaureguiberry

stops.name: Areguá, into Paraguay
stops.date_confidence: attested, Spanish Wikipedia; the year is a placeholder.
stops.campa: A shrine to Gil stands at Areguá, in the country he was shipped across the Paraná to fight against. The men he was conscripted to kill are the great-grandfathers of the people who now leave him candles. Nothing in the devotion marks the reversal or needs to: what the poor of both banks recognize in him is not a nationality but a conscript, taken from home by an authority with a grudge, killed by the same authority, and useful afterwards to anybody in trouble.
suggested_refs: The Areguá shrine, Paraguay

stops.name: Tarija, up the labour routes
stops.date_confidence: attested, Spanish Wikipedia; the year is a placeholder.
stops.campa: The red reaches Bolivia. Tarija, in the Andean south, keeps a shrine to a Correntino gaucho two thousand kilometres from any country he could have ridden, carried up the migrant labour routes that run in both directions across that border. He arrives in the pockets of harvest workers and bricklayers, along with the mate and the music, and he is absorbed into a religious landscape already crowded with saints the Vatican never approved. Nobody there needs the biography. The function travels without it.
suggested_refs: The Tarija shrine, Bolivia

stops.name: The Carretera Austral, shrines on a Chilean road
stops.date_confidence: reconstruction; Spanish Wikipedia reports roadside shrines along the Carretera Austral. The coordinate is a point on a road running hundreds of kilometres, not a specific sanctuary, and the year is a placeholder.
stops.campa: On the gravel of the Carretera Austral, in Chilean Patagonia, red cloth appears at the side of the road. It comes over the Andes with truckers and travellers, and it does the same work here that it does on the routes of Corrientes: it marks the place where somebody wanted protection on a bad stretch. The cult of Gil has turned into a road religion, whatever it started as. It grows wherever people drive long distances alone and are aware that the distance can kill them.

stops.name: The BP-5002 outside Barcelona, the furthest cross
stops.date_confidence: attested as to the location, Spanish Wikipedia: 'a las afueras de Barcelona, km 5,5 de la carretera BP-5002', the Alella to Òrrius road in the Maresme. The coordinate approximates that road at the stated kilometre; a research-pool value placing the shrine in Barcelona city centre, about 18 km away, was discarded. The year is a placeholder.
stops.campa: At kilometre five and a half of a small provincial road in the Maresme, above Barcelona, Argentine emigrants raise a shrine to the Gauchito. It is ten thousand kilometres from the espinillo and it is on a roadside, which is the only specification the devotion has ever had. The furthest recorded point of the cult is not a cathedral and not a chapel. It is a bend on a secondary road out of a European city, tended by people who left Argentina and did not leave this.

stops.name: Corrientes, Entre la luna y el sol
stops.date_confidence: attested; the exhibition, its date and its coordinate are inherited from the atlas file for Leo Chiachio.
stops.campa: In the city of Corrientes itself, the provincial capital that gave the whole territory its name, its courts and its founding charter, the devotion needs no importing. It is simply the seat of the government whose countryside produced Gil, conscripted him, condemned him, and later tied a red flag to every road running out of it. The capital and the camp have always been the same province seen from two ends: one the seat of law, the other the ground the law reached out to punish and could not, in the end, hold onto.
suggested_refs: Leo Chiachio, Entre la luna y el sol, Corrientes, 2015

stops.name: Argentina, a quarter of a country
stops.date_confidence: attested at one remove; English Wikipedia cites survey data for roughly 23 percent of Argentines identifying as devotees. The underlying survey was not reached and the figure is taken on the encyclopedia's citation.
stops.campa: A survey finds that something near a quarter of Argentines count themselves devotees of the Gauchito. That is a larger constituency than most political parties in the country, and it belongs to a man the Church does not recognize, whose birth year is unknown, whose grave cannot be located and whose entire biography is oral. Read the other way round, the figure counts how many people in Argentina have needed something badly and had nowhere official to take it. The number describes the askers better than it describes him.
suggested_refs: The 2019 survey of devotion to Gauchito Gil, cited but not traced to its surveying body
